extracted.intended_audience: CIA legal counsel and agency policymakers (Office of General Counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of substantive provisions in the Proposed Administrative Procedure Act of 1967 focusing on changes to agency rulemaking and adjudicative procedures, rights of persons appearing before agencies, and exemptions for national defense/foreign policy. Intended to identify which provisions directly affect the CIA and how the Agency should treat exemptions and procedural conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of policymaking and adjudicative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill overhauls administrative procedures by separating policymaking functions from adjudicative functions; it 'relieves policymakers from the responsibility of deciding cases as well as making policy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes organizational and procedural separation so that those who make policy are not responsible for deciding individual cases. This is presented as a general structural reform of agency processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on rulemaking to avoid ad hoc decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill encourages increased rulemaking by policymakers in order to avoid the prevalence of ad hoc decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should favor promulgated rules over case-by-case ad hoc adjudication to create consistent, predictable agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expeditious adjudicative procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: In the adjudicative area, the bill provides for expeditious court procedures such as specific pleadings, prehearing conferences and interlocutory appeals so that cases may be decided with greater celerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural tools listed (specific pleadings, prehearing conferences, interlocutory appeals) are intended to speed resolution. Agencies should adopt or accommodate these devices where applicable to reduce delay in adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to counsel in agency proceedings and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill gives all persons the right to counsel whether they appear voluntarily or involuntarily before any agency, and whether their appearance is in the course of an agency investigation or an agency proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This right extends to contexts such as report of survey proceedings and accident investigations; agencies must permit representation by counsel in both investigatory and adjudicatory settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: National defense/foreign policy exemptions with 'greatest extent practicable' conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency or action exempted by the bill because national defense or foreign policy is involved is required to 'conform to the greatest extent practicable' to the procedures of the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where exemptions apply, agencies should follow bill procedures as much as practicable—meaning partial conformity is expected when full application is constrained by defense/foreign-policy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption from public information and rulemaking sections for defense reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agency (CIA) is exempted from the public information and rulemaking sections of the bill for reasons of national defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memorandum notes this exemption would have slight impact on the CIA because the public information and rulemaking sections primarily stress disclosure (publication of proceedings, opinions, and orders), which may already be constrained by the Agency's mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited direct applicability to CIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Only two provisions of the bill appear to apply directly to CIA: the right to counsel and the 'greatest extent practicable' conformity requirement for exempted actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect on the Agency is expected to be slight; the Office of General Counsel should consider operational implications (e.g., counsel in internal investigations) but recognize broad exemptions for defense/foreign policy.
